item.title: 'Stupendously large' primordial black holes ruled out as a dark matter source
item.description: Primordial black holes are hypothetical objects that could have formed directly from dense clumps of matter in the very early universe. If they exist, their dramatic origins would set them apart from the black holes we see today, which form when massive stars collapse. Some theories suggest that "stupendously large" primordial black holes could account for a significant share of the universe's elusive dark matter.

item.title: Could primordial black holes hold the key to dark matter?
item.description: Some black holes may be older than the stars themselves. And their existence could help solve one of the biggest mysteries in physics: dark matter

item.title: Using Vibrations and AI, Future Robotic Missions Could Handle Buried Rocks Autonomously
item.description: Mechanical engineering assistant professor Erik Komendera developed a method that combines vibrations and AI to determine how deeply a rock is buried, helping robots clear terrain more efficiently.

item.title: Robot successfully builds space structure in first autonomous construction demo
item.description: A robotic truss builder that was conceived, designed and built by Caltech researchers has successfully built a structure in space—without the help of astronauts—for the first time. The truss builder, part of DARPA's Novel Orbital and Moon Manufacturing, Materials, and Mass-efficient Design (NOM4D) program, consists of an autonomous manipulator that picks up struts and joints held in nearby dispensers to repeatedly assemble identical sections, or bays, of a perimeter truss.

item.title: Exoplanets Can't Hide From The JWST's 'Digital Twin'
item.description: Finding dim exoplanets hidden in the glare of their stars is an ongoing challenge in astronomy. Telescopes use coronagraphs to block out starlight, but even they have their limitations. Researchers have developed a new technique with the JWST that can find dim exoplanets more easily than ever.

item.title: First known 'disappearing planet' has a neighbor that makes it wobble like a top
item.description: UCLA-led astronomers have discovered the first known "disappearing planet" about 1,000 light-years away. The planet, TOI-2535 b, is a "hot Jupiter," a gas giant that orbits extremely close to its host star. TOI-2535 b whips around its star in only 8.25 days—10 times faster than the 88 days that Mercury takes to go around our sun once.

item.title: Two nearby rocky worlds could offer alien astronomers views of planets appearing to reverse course
item.description: Aliens have long been a staple of science fiction. Yet the possibility of intelligent life beyond Earth is more than a matter of imagination—it is also a subject of serious scientific inquiry. Professor Woong-bae Zee of Sejong University's School of Liberal Studies has recently published an astronomy paper that places the word "alien" front and center.

item.title: Nov. 9, 1939: The birth of Carl Sagan
item.description: Nobody did more to popularize astronomy than American astronomer Carl Sagan, who was born Nov. 9, 1939, in New York. The landmark 1980 television series Cosmos: A Personal Voyage, which he cowrote and narrated, has been viewed by more than half a billion people. item.title: There may be a new dwarf planet just beyond Pluto
item.description: Astronomers spotted what appears to be a dwarf planet in the outer solar system using the Vera C. Rubin Observatory – if confirmed, it joins a small and exclusive club

item.title: Long-lived mineral grains can be invaluable for reconstructing impact events, but the stories are complex
item.description: Reconstructing impact events on Earth and other planetary bodies, including the moon, is crucial for understanding how the solar system evolved and how planets develop.

item.title: An Artificial CORTEX to Guide Satellite Rescue Missions
item.description: Thousands of so-called zombie satellites orbit Earth in the critical Low-Earth Orbit regime. They're either inactive or have stopped alerting other satellites to their presence. Researchers are building a system called CORTEX that can guide a repair satellite to autonomously dock with these zombies.

item.title: A Common Food Emulsifier Could Solve One of Rocketry’s Oldest Fuel Problems
item.description: In propulsion system design, engineers have long faced a trade-off between solid and liquid rocket fuels. Each has advantages and disadvantages, and in an effort to try to min/max the efficacy of different types of fuel, researchers have long placed an emphasis on a hybrid between solids and liquids - in other words they’ve been working with gels. item.title: Game theory helps SETI search for alien civilizations
item.description: The search for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI) is mostly concerned with where to look for technosignatures from another civilization. Between 2012 and 2015, SETI's Project Phoenix targeted about 1,000 sun-like stars for signs of intelligent life. But where to look might not be as important as when to look, according to scientists at SETI.

item.title: Wacky magnetic fields of ice giants may stem from conductivity changes in their deep interiors
item.description: When NASA's Voyager 2 robotic probe flew by Uranus and Neptune in the 1980s, it uncovered an anomaly: their magnetic fields are highly disordered, unlike Earth's, which has well-defined north and south poles.

item.title: Asteroids' Oddball Shapes Make Deflecting Them Challenging
item.description: In a pinch, we could use a stand-off nuclear blast to redirect a dangerous asteroid on short notice. There's no atmospheric shock wave in space, but the x-ray pulse could still deflect the space rock. But asteroids aren't round and uniform, so their weird shapes make it difficult.

item.title: For students with their sights set on space medicine, a new community takes flight
item.description: MIT’s Doctors Without Gravity club connects health and space science enthusiasts.

item.title: Read an extract from Dark Eden by Chris Beckett
item.description: In this extract from Chris Beckett’s Dark Eden, the November read for the New Scientist Book Club, we meet some of the inhabitants of a dark planet that drifts outside the Milky Way, descendants of two astronauts marooned there over a century earlier

item.title: Robotic “SuperLimbs” could help moonwalkers recover from falls
item.description: A new MIT system could help astronauts conserve energy and extend missions on the lunar surface.

item.title: Study: Life’s building blocks are surprisingly stable in Venus-like conditions
item.description: Results suggest the clouds of Venus could be hospitable for some forms of life.

item.title: Why the Drake equation is still important 65 years after its creation
item.description: The Drake equation provides a way to guess how many aliens we might be able to communicate with, but it’s also a prime example of the importance of scientific guessing, says columnist Leah Crane

item.title: The next generation’s guide to the new space economy
item.description: An industry report published by students in an MIT aerospace entrepreneurship class lays out guidance for aspiring space leaders and investors.

item.title: Turning up the heat on next-generation semiconductors
item.description: Research sheds light on the properties of novel materials that could be used in electronics operating in extremely hot environments.

item.title: Margaret Hamilton, computing pioneer who led software development for the Apollo program, dies at 90
item.description: Over two decades at MIT, Hamilton forged new paths in computer science and engineering. Her groundbreaking work included leading the team that programmed the first computers that took humans to the moon.

item.title: How to design a space habitat that supports its residents’ mental health
item.description: A new online platform helps engineers look beyond survival mode when designing habitats for extreme living conditions.

item.title: Supporting mission-driven space innovation, for Earth and beyond
item.description: Aurelia Institute, founded by a team from MIT, serves as a research lab, an education and outreach center, and a policy hub for the space industry.
